conbody.p: The Copyright Alternative Small-Claims Enforcement or the “CASE” Act, signed into law December 2020, and is estimated to go into full effect beginning June of 2022.

The act creates a small-claims court within the United States Copyright Office known as the Copyright Claims Board (CCB). The CCB is a three-member tribunal whose job is to review claims and make a determination within 90 days, expediting the federal process which can take months or even years. The CCB is expected to review claims of infringement, claims for declaration of noninfringement (the issue of a legal statement that affirms a party is not liable for infringement), and claims of misrepresentation concerning DMCA takedown notices. Holders can file claims through the new CCB website for around $100. They may ask for $15,000 in damages per infringed work, with damages capped at $30,000. This system will be opt-in, meaning use of the CCB is not required. If the defendant so chooses, they can proceed down the federal court path. The literature of the bill itself and the newly minted CCB website tout a user-friendly quality to the court — accessibility for the layman, who is not explicitly encouraged to appear without representation, but is made aware that representation is not necessary.

image.alt: Left-aligned seal featuring an eagle in the middle of a white letter "C." Right-aligned white text on a navy background that reads "CCB.gov Copyright Claims Board."

conbody.p: Where does the concern lie in appearing in court without legal representation, with $30,000 on the line, in a system where holders need only pay $100 to file claims of infringement? If the goal is to make copyright litigation more accessible, the CASE Act, only does so for the holder. With the ever-increasing use of MDJD litigation, those who want to make a few dollars on the side fishing for illegal downloaders can now do so for cheap, racking up claims in order to shake down the consumer. If holders once found profits daring the consumer to violate their copyright, this will only increase tenfold under the CASE Act. Moreover, those who do so would certainly not risk appearing in court without legal representation, leaving the defendant at a huge disadvantage when facing the CCB should they be convinced by the Act’s rhetoric. The CCB’s determination is final, leaving the defendant with no ability to appeal. While $30,000 is significantly less than the willful infringement fine of $150,000, a CNBC article published in 2021 states that only 39% of Americans can afford even a $1,000 unexpected expense. Thirty thousand dollars in addition to all the accrued legal fees that come with any form of litigation still has the potential to financially ruin the average American citizen. With so many Americans willing to knowingly violate copyright, the implementation of the CASE Act leaves the average one uninformed and at huge risk for being exploited financially, positioning large holders to increase their profits through settlement.
